story:colchis.en:
## Tragic: "Two Brothers in Ambri's Furrow" (1899)

> "I didn't kill him. I brought him home. And home would not take him."
>
> — Levy-man Giorgi, from an interrogation record

Giorgi's elder brother, Levan, worked in the mine until the mine closed. The winter passed in hunger. In spring Levan vanished, and their mother said
he had gone to sea for work. Giorgi knew perfectly well she was lying.

In the Spring of Blood, when the Grand Harness first moved, Giorgi stood in Ambri's Furrow. The rebels came out of the fog — in ragged uniforms,
with chains. In the third rank Giorgi recognised his brother's back: as children they had both fallen from a walnut tree together, and Levan had broken his shoulder blade so badly that one
shoulder still sat higher than the other.

Giorgi did not fire. He laid down his rifle and walked out into the fog, calling him by name. Levan turned, and for a moment they both stood there — two brothers, in two uniforms,
in one furrow.

Then the shooting started along the front, and Levan fell. Whose bullet it was — no one knows.

Giorgi carried his brother's body down to the village. The village elder saw the heretic's mark on his chest and said he would not be buried in this
earth. Levan was buried outside the village, by the roadside. Giorgi goes there on every leave — and tells no one why.

## Heroic: "Orovela" (1913)

> "An ox doesn't listen to an engine. An ox listens to a song. It was the same in Ambri's day."
>
> — Bego the ox-driver

Ambri's Ox — a bronze steam ox, one of the twelve — served the front for six more years after the Winter of Wire. In the autumn of
1913 its boiler went out in the middle of a gas cloud. Forty wounded lay on its bed.

Bego the ox-driver was seventy years old. He took off his gas mask so his voice would carry, stepped out in front of the ox and began to sing **orovela** — the old
ploughing song with which his grandfather had led real oxen.

The engineers say the boiler lit by itself at that moment. The ox-drivers say the ox recognised the song. Bego walked two versts through the gas, singing
and coughing, and the ox followed — slowly, along the Furrow, exactly as it had carried Ambri forty-two years before.

All forty wounded arrived alive. Bego died in the hospital three days later. Now, when Ambri's Ox moves, the ox-drivers sing orovela —
and no one says it is superstition.

story:iberia.en:
## Tragic: "The Mail Shirt" (1871–1914)

> "It always comes back. The mail shirt always comes back."
>
> — the words of a Khevsur woman

A Khevsur woman, Mzia, had one mail shirt in her house. Her father-in-law put it on on the Night of Opening, in 1871, and went to Qursha's Ravine.
The shirt came back in the autumn — a comrade brought it, folded, bloody. Mzia washed it, scrubbed off the rust and set the broken rings back in
by hand.

In 1899, in the Spring of Blood, her husband put on the shirt. He stood before the Grand Harness as the city trampled the trenches. The shirt came back in summer,
folded again.

Mzia washed it again and set the rings in again. This time the new rings were a different colour, and the shirt became two-toned.

In the spring of 1914, when the Grand Harness moved toward Ambri's grave, her grandson, sixteen-year-old Gio, put on the shirt.
Mzia walked him to the door and said nothing. Since then she watches the road every evening.

The mail shirt always comes back. Mzia knows it. She is waiting for something else.

## Heroic: "Bero's Bark" (1906)

> "For the first time in its life the dog barked at an officer. We scolded the dog. The dog was right."
>
> — notes of the Spasalari's adjutant

The Tushetian shepherd Tamar's nagazi, **Bero**, was a calm dog. In five years it had never once barked at a person — only at a devi-spawn,
and once at a bear.

In the winter of 1906 a coalition liaison officer arrived at headquarters with great ceremony: he brought new maps and the recommendation of an old engineer
from the Age of Sealing. As he went into the Spasalari's tent, Bero leapt out of the snow and blocked the door so that the officer stepped back.

Everyone said the dog had gone wild. Tamar pulled Bero away and apologised. But at night, when the officer thought everyone was asleep, Bero
barked again — this time by the storehouse where the new maps were kept. Tamar came out and saw the officer changing the line of a mountain path
on the map — exactly so that the next day's detachment would walk straight into the devis' ravine.

The Listener never made it to interrogation — he killed himself. Every map was re-checked. Since then no new person enters Iberian headquarters
until a nagazi has sniffed him — and no one finds this rule funny.

story:hell.en:
> Stories of the dark side through their own eyes: "heroism" for them is obedience; tragedy — whatever obedience cannot contain.

## Tragic: "No. 4471" (1902)

> "A recruit needs no name. A name is the enemy of order."
>
> — from the Legion's regulations

Recruit **4471** grew in a flask, like all the rest: the same face, the same voice, the same number on the arm. It was taught
the volley, the formation, the advance. Nothing more.

In the winter of 1902 the Legion took a Colchian levy-man prisoner, and 4471 was ordered to guard him. The levy-man talked all night — about his mother, his village,
his wife, whose name was **Natia**. 4471 asked what "Natia" was. The levy-man told it: a name. What they call you when they love you.

In the morning the prisoner was taken away. 4471 went to the Marquis — the first recruit in the Legion's history to speak without an order — and asked for a name.

The Marquis looked at it for a long time. Then he ordered the recruit **returned to the flask** — "due to a defect". No. 4472, which took its place, was exactly
the same. But the Legion's chronicler, as he wrote down the order, hesitated for the first time in his life — and in the margin of the record, in small letters, he wrote:
"Natia".

## Heroic: "Halphas's Seven Nights" (1908)

> "The tower was built in one night. The tower was held for seven nights. The Legion carried out its order."
>
> — the Legion's report, in full

In the Winter of Wire one file of Halphas's Garrison-Builders was given an order: in one night, build a tower in the middle of no man's land and hold it
until the Legion reached them.

They built the tower by night, in steam armour, without a sound. By morning the tower stood. The Legion did not come — the road was blocked by gas and by Iberia's Thunderbolt Gunners.

The garrison-builders held the tower for seven nights. Supplies ran out on the third day. On the fifth day their commander — a rank below Marquis — gave
an order: strip the plates from the dead's armour and hammer them into the tower wall.

On the eighth morning the Legion arrived. It found nine alive in the tower — out of forty. The Marquis wrote one sentence in his report. In the legions that is called great
praise. But the Colchian scouts who watched the tower from afar still remember: in seven nights not one sound came from the tower — no
screaming, no singing, no orders.

story:harness.en:
> The heretics come from every nation. Many of them were not brought by evil — but by hunger, anger or a promise.

## Tragic: "Bread from the Harness-Lord" (1889–1904)

> "He told us the children would have bread. The children had bread."
>
> — a rebel's last words, on the steps of the altar

Dato was a miner. When the mine closed in 1889, his three children barely made it through the winter. In spring quiet people came to the village
and said: **the Harness-Lord** needs workers underground. The wage — bread. Every week, for the family.

Dato went. The bread came — every week, for fifteen years. Dato worked at the Grand Harness's boilers, then in the trenches, then in the ranks of the rebels.
He no longer asked whom he fought for. He knew only whom he worked for.

In 1904, after Dragon's Field, when the Grand Harness fell back and had no prisoners left, the altar needed fresh blood. The lists
were filled with the names of those who had been "in debt" the longest. Dato's name was first.

He climbed the steps of the altar strangely calm. His daughter, who was working as a nurse in Colchis at the time, learned of it only ten years later
— from a wounded heretic who had known her father. "He used to say you had bread," the heretic said. The daughter dressed his wound
and made no answer.

## Heroic: "The Night of the Harness-Slaves" (1910)

> "The chain is one. If we all pull together — the chain will follow us."
>
> — the words of a captive smith

The city of the Grand Harness is hauled by prisoners in chains — two hundred, three hundred people on one chain, beside the devis. In 1910, after the Night of the Sky-Ships,
the city stood still for four months. In those four months the prisoners learned to talk to each other — in whispers, in thirteen languages.

One captive smith — an Italian named **Bruno** — checked every link of the chain by hand and found one that rust had eaten through.

When the city moved again, at night, at the edge of a ravine, Bruno gave the signal. Three hundred people at once, in one instant, pulled the chain **backward**. The rusted link
snapped. One section of the Harness — and with it two chained devis — slid into the ravine.

Half the prisoners died that same night. Half escaped into the darkness. Fifty reached the trenches of Colchis. Bruno was not among them —
he stayed by the chain to unlock the last man's shackles. After that night the Grand Harness put a double guard on every chain — and forbade the prisoners
to speak to one another.

story:listeners.en:
### Tragic: "The Gift" (1871)
**Heinrich** was a Listener for twenty years and for twenty years was proud of his work: the seal he built protected his home town, and the town raised
a monument to him. On the Night of Opening he opened his lock, like all the rest. In the morning he walked through the town — and by his monument, in the square, the first thing
he saw was what had come up out of the seal. He never went back to the Brotherhood. He stayed in the town, clearing rubble, for nine years, until someone recognised him.

### Heroic (through their own eyes): "The Empty Uniform" (1902)
The Brotherhood's sleeper **Irina** lived for five years in the Colchian levy under a false name. In 1902 her company was about to be taken by the heretics —
for the altar. The Brotherhood's order was: do not interfere. Irina led the company out at night by a marsh path that only the Brotherhood knew, and in the morning
she vanished — leaving her uniform in the trench, folded. In the Brotherhood they call her "the lost one". In the company — "our twentieth", and they leave her place in the rank empty.

story:kajeti.en:
### Tragic: "Too Good a Craft" (1890)
The kaji smith **Urma** made a captive soldier a new hand — of cast iron, with silver joints, the best she had ever made. The soldier
escaped, with the new hand, and went back to his unit. Two years later he stood at the gate of Kajeti, with the same hand, breaking down the gate. From behind the gate Urma recognised
her own work — and could not lift her hammer. Zarda took her forge away from her. The kajis say: "Don't make it so good that it works against you."

### Heroic (through their own eyes): "The Forge Under the Avalanche" (1897)
An avalanche buried the forge in the Kajeti valley, and twenty kajis and two hundred prisoners were trapped inside. The kajis did not let the forge go out: for a whole month they beat their hammers,
in one rhythm, so that the forge's heat melted a tunnel through the snow. The prisoners went out first — the kajis decided so: "the material must survive".
Half of the prisoners stayed in Kajeti of their own free will. Zarda says it was the best bargain Kajeti ever struck.

story:ring.en:
### Tragic: "The Letter No One Could Read" (1906)
**Tomasz**, a soldier of a Tithe detachment, lived for three years in a trench with a boy whose language he did not understand. They talked in signs, ate from one bowl
and guarded each other's backs. When the boy was killed, Tomasz found a letter in his pocket — to his mother. For a year he searched for an interpreter who knew that
language. At last he found one. The letter said: "There's a man here who doesn't know my language. But he is my brother." Tomasz took the letter to the mother himself —
and read it, in two languages, in the interpreter's voice.

### Heroic: "Forty Voices" (1910)
During a night attack the battalion's telephone line was cut, and forty detachments stood along the line, with forty languages. The heretics shouted false orders —
in every language the Listeners had learned. **The interpreters** walked the line on foot and had every detachment sing the same song — the battalion's
song, which everyone knows by heart, with the same tune in every language. Where the song was heard, the order was real. The false voices drowned in the song.

story:hellenic.en:
### Tragic: "The Bronze Son" (1891)
The old engineer **Stavros** assembled automaton phalanxes in the forge of Hephaestus. His son was killed on the shore of the hydras, and that winter Stavros
cast one automaton in his son's likeness — the face, the walk, the tilt of the head. The automaton fought like all the others. But every night, when the phalanx
returned to camp, it stepped out of the rank and stopped at Stavros's door — silent, until morning. The League issued an order: melt the automaton
down, the front needed the bronze. Stavros lit the furnace himself. Since then he has never given a new automaton a face.

### Heroic: "The Eye of the Storm" (1897)
When Typhon's storm neared the shore, only one of the Cyclops cannons of the Storm Wall was left whole, and of its crew — only
young **Eirini**. In the heart of the storm, they said, hides the eye of Typhon. Eirini braced the lens against the wind, waited two hours
and fired the moment the wind dropped for a single second. The storm broke apart. The cannon was found melted, Eirini — beneath it, alive. She still
assembles phalanxes — and sets a lens in each one in place of an eye.

story:northern.en:
### Tragic: "The Horn That Fell Silent" (1881)
Heimdall's hornblower **Einar** stood above the fjord, and he had his orders: do not sound until the wolves cross the bridge — so as not to raise
a false alarm. The wolves did not come over the bridge — they came over the ice, below the bridge. Einar saw them and hesitated: the order
was about the bridge. When he sounded, half the town was asleep. Since then every hornblower of the North has one rule: "When in doubt — sound."

### Heroic: "Astrid's Oath" (1902)
A new chain, woven "from impossible things", had to be wrapped around Fenrir — but the wolf would not let the chain near until someone put a hand
in its jaws, as in the old story. **Astrid** — a veteran of Tyr's One-Handed, whose one hand was already steam — stepped forward and
put in the other, living hand. The chain was bound. The wolf bit the hand off. Astrid now fights with two steam hands and says the oath is now
doubly bound.

story:celtic.en:
### Tragic: "A Friend's Eye" (1898)
There was a traitor among Lugh's Slingers, and **Rowan** found him: **Conall**, with whom he had slung stones since childhood. Rowan could have
taken him alive, but Conall stood on the shore, at the sound of a Fomorian boat, giving a signal. Rowan fired — exactly as they had learned together.
Rowan tells this story to no one — and no longer picks up a sling.

### Heroic: "Three Blows" (1913)
The bullet for Balor's eye had to be forged with three blows, without a pause — exactly as in the myth. The Fomorians attacked Goibniu's forge, and
the master smith — **Brigid** — was hit by a bullet after the first blow. She struck the second blow fallen on one knee. The third — her apprentice,
who held her hand on the hammer. The bullet is ready. In the forge it bears the marks of two hands.

story:finnish.en:
### Tragic: "The Mother of the Twilight" (1914)
**Elina's** mother was born in the first winter of the Twilight and has never seen the real sun — only Ilmarinen's steam sun, which shines but does not
warm. When the town debated putting out the steam sun, her mother told Elina: "Put it out. I lived in the twilight. You — must not." Elina carried her
voice to the assembly. On the day the decision was made, her mother died in a cold room — in the light of the steam sun.

### Heroic: "A Song for the Mountain" (1909)
Väinämöinen's Singers knew the sun was hidden in Louhi's mountain — but the mountain had no door. Thirteen singers stood at the mountain's foot and
sang for thirteen nights, with one voice, until the rock followed the song — and a crack appeared. Light came out of the crack, for just one second.
Thirteen of the singers went, nine came back. Now everyone knows where the sun is. But the thirteen nights are still needed.

story:britain.en:
### Tragic: "The Last Lesson" (1886)
The school of Beowulf's Heirs stood on the edge of the fen: forty pupils, one old teacher, one hall. One night the hall was attacked by spawn
risen from the mere — exactly as in the epic. The teacher took the children up to the loft and threw down the ladder. In the morning the only one alive
was **Wilfred**, the smallest, who had climbed to the loft last and seen everything. He now commands the fen scouts, and his detachment
never sleeps in a hall.

### Heroic: "One Lantern" (1912)
The mother's hall lies beneath the mere, and, according to the epic, one may only go down there alone. Wilfred went down in a steam diving helmet with one lantern.
The lantern went out in the third minute. He went along the wall, feeling his way by hand, until he reached the lock. The lock has not yet broken —
but Wilfred knows the way, and on the shore of the mere there is now a rope that runs all the way to the hall.

story:gaul.en:
### Tragic: "The Iberian Rifle" (1903)
**Héloïse** learned lightning technology in Iberia and spoke Georgian. When it came out that there was a lock in the first lightning rifles, many in Gaul
said the Iberians had put it there — and Héloïse with them. Her detachment was moved elsewhere on the front, and her letters to Iberia were not delivered.
The lock, as was later proved, was put there by a Listener engineer — a Gaul. No one ever apologised to Héloïse. She still speaks two languages,
but the second — only to herself.

### Heroic: "A Wheel on the Bridge" (1910)
The Tarasque was moving upriver, toward the last bridge, beyond which lay the town. Taranis's Wheel — a lightning-wheeled fortress-engine — should not have been able
to reach the bridge: it was far too heavy. The crew drove onto the bridge anyway, and the bridge collapsed — right on top of the monster. The Wheel
fell into the river along with the Tarasque, and all night lightning flashed from the riverbed. The Tarasque fled wounded. Six of the crew came up.

story:italy.en:
### Tragic: "Father's House" (1895)
**Giulia's** teacher, master **Anselmo**, was the oldest smith in Vulcan's forge. When it came out that Cacus was Vulcan's son,
Anselmo said: "We are fighting a god's son. This is a betrayal of the father's house." One night he went down into the caves, to the heretics. Giulia saw him
a year later — as a smith tending Cacus's fire. Anselmo recognised her and waved, as he used to in the forge. Giulia did not
fire. The neighbouring crew — did.

### Heroic: "The Mouth of the Cave" (1907)
Cacus came up out of his cave, and only three streets were left before the town. Giulia's crew rolled a field gun into the mouth of the cave — into the heart
of the fire — and fired at the monster from behind, so that the cave's vault came down. Cacus was trapped inside, part of his fire — under the stone.
The crew were burned by the fire, but lived. In the town that street now bears their name — all six of them.

story:polianitsy.en:
### Tragic: "Sleeping in the Ice" (1913)
**Vasilisa** returned to her home village after thirteen years — on the trail of Koschei's egg. In the middle of the village, under the ice, lay her father — just
as he had left twenty years before: young, calm, eyes closed. The ice would not break, neither with an axe nor with fire. Vasilisa laid her hand on the ice
and stood there a long time. Then she left — because now she knew: the men are not dead. And until the needle is broken, they will not wake either.

### Heroic: "One on the Bridge" (1909)
Only a few polianitsy come to the Wound each year. That autumn, when the rebels moved toward the bridge over the Furrow, only one
polianitsa stood on the bridge — **Daria**, on horseback, with an old bogatyr's sword. She stood there all night. In the morning, when the Colchians came, the bridge was still whole.
Daria could barely sit her horse for her wounds. The Colchians lifted her down from the bridge by hand. Before winter set in she went home, as always.
The bridge is now called **"Daria's Bridge"** — and every autumn someone lays flowers on it.

story:armenian.en:
### Tragic: "The Aralez's Last Lick" (1896)
**Nare's** steam aralez — a mechanical dog whose tongue seeps living water — had revived the fallen three times. The fourth time, the fallen
boy had been wounded by vishap blood, and the dog licked the wound anyway. The boy got to his feet. The aralez — did not. The vishap blood ate its mechanism
from the inside. Nare carried the dog down the mountain on her own back. She has built a new aralez since, but gives no one the old one's name.

### Heroic: "Tork's Stones" (1904)
On Dragon's Field the Tork Colossus hurled stones from its back, and the stones were passed up to its back by hand by hundreds of people — highlanders down from the villages,
who stood in a chain from the mountain to the field. They passed stone after stone all day, every hand — one stone. When the Grand Harness fell back,
many did not know who had won the battle. The highlanders knew: every stone the Colossus threw had once been in their hands.

story:oghuz.en:
### Tragic: "Flesh for the Bird" (1912)
**Aydın** came up from the underworld lame — as in the tale, he fed the Zümrüd bird with his own flesh. But **Emre**, his childhood friend, had gone down the well
with him. When the bird ran out of food and Aydın had no strength left, Emre said: "You carry the lock up.
I'll stay, so the bird has less to carry." And he let go. Now every morning Aydın goes to the well and leaves a piece of bread there.

### Heroic: "One Song, Three Languages" (1907)
On the coldest night of the Winter of Wire the trenches of three sectors were all about to collapse at once — Georgian, Armenian and Oghuz. The night
was silent and everyone feared the others would abandon the line. Then in the Oghuz trench someone began the song of **Köroğlu**. In the Armenian trench
they took up the same story in Armenian, in the Georgian — in Georgian. All night the three trenches sang one story in three languages. In the morning the line was whole.
Since then the liaison officers of the three sectors share one password — the name of Kırat.

story:nile.en:
### Tragic: "He Trusted the Clock" (1902)
The old timekeeper **Omar** counted the hours of the night for forty years by voice, by the stars and by heart. When a new coalition clock was fitted to the Sun-Boat,
Omar was told: your counting is no longer needed. One night his count and the clock disagreed — Omar said dawn was near,
the clock — that it was still early. The boat obeyed the clock and stayed in the desert an hour longer. Apep used that hour. Omar stayed
with the boat. Twelve years later **Nadia** found his notes — and in them the hour that did not exist.

### Heroic: "The Prow of the Boat" (1894)
The crew of Set's Spearmen stands at the prow of the boat, where Set stood in the myth. That night Apep's head struck the boat three times. The crew held the spear-cannon
on the prow by hand when its mount broke. They stayed at the prow all night, bracing the cannon with their hands and firing. In the morning the sun rose.
Two of the five were alive, and five names are now carved into the prow of the boat.

story:yellow_river.en:
### Tragic: "The Old Master's Notebook" (1913)
In 1866 the old master **Chen** spoke out against the dam: "This is Gun's way." He was dismissed from service. For forty-seven years, every
year, he wrote down the height of the dam in a notebook — and each time added on the same page: "The water is going down." His granddaughter **Lin**
found the notebook the day after his death — and thanks to it proved the lock. The master was one day short of seeing them believe it.

### Heroic: "The Ninth Head" (1909)
Xiangliu has nine heads, and on the drawings on the tripod one of the heads is drawn differently — the old masters said it is the weak one. When
the serpent came up onto the bank, **Lin** compared the heads in the drawing with the living monster while the riflemen died around her. On the eighth head
she was wrong. On the ninth — not. One precise volley sent the serpent to the bottom. The tripod's drawing now has a new line — in Lin's hand.

story:japan_isles.en:
### Tragic: "The Treasure Captain" (1871)
The captain of the 1867 expedition, **Kenji**, came home a hero — with the oni's treasure, exactly as in the tale. For four years people
stopped him in the street to thank him. On the Night of Opening the gate opened in the city's vault — where his treasure was kept.
Kenji understood what he had brought home. In the morning his boat was gone from the harbour. He put to sea alone, toward the oni's island — and never came back.

### Heroic: "Three Companions Under the City" (1899)
The oni seized a school cellar beneath the city, with forty children. The army could not get into the tunnels. Then three scouts went — **with a dog, a monkey
and a steam glider**, as in the tale. The dog found the way, the monkey went across the ceiling, the glider showed the way out of the cellar. All forty children
came out. Since then every scout detachment wears three badges — a dog, a monkey and a pheasant.

story:korea.en:
### Tragic: "Grandmother's Tale" (1910)
**Mi-rae's** grandmother told everyone that the mountain crystals were the imugis' pearls. In the village no one paid her any attention: an old woman, old
tales. She died in the winter when the first imugi turned into a dragon and the water swept the valley away. Mi-rae wrote down the tale in her words and
took it to front headquarters. There everyone now knows her grandmother's name.

### Heroic: "A Wager with the Dokkaebi" (1914)
The dokkaebi offered Mi-rae a wrestling match: if she won, they would hide the crystals. A dokkaebi, they say, is always weak on one leg. Mi-rae wrestled
all night, trying a different leg each time — until she found the weak one. The dokkaebi fell over and laughed. All seven crystals
vanished from the mountains in one night. In the morning the imugis climbed to the peaks and found bare stone.

story:mongolia.en:
### Tragic: "The Closed Station" (1868)
The örtöö station keeper **Bata** changed horses for the messengers for thirty years, day and night. When the iron line came, the station was closed and the horses
sold. Bata was hired as a line watchman — of the very line that had taken his station. In the winter of 1871 a sand worm followed the iron, and Bata
was found along the line. Horses stand in his station again now — his grandson changes them.

### Heroic: "The Örtöö Race" (1914)
**Saran** compared the map of the attacks with the map of the lines and understood: every line leads to the gate. The news would take four days to reach front headquarters
by telegraph — but the telegraph was already down. Saran went by örtöö: thirteen stations, thirteen horses, two days and two nights without sleep.
Some stations were empty, and herders gave her a horse. The news arrived in time. The next day they began cutting the lines.

story:balkans.en:
## Tragic: "The Most Faithful Gunner" (1903)

The village ranger **Stoyan** served his hail cannon more faithfully than anyone in the valley: when a cloud appeared, his cannon was the first
to fire and the last to fall silent. Of all the valley, his village was hit by the most hail, and Stoyan thought it was because he fired too little.
He fired more. In the summer of 1903 the hail destroyed every field in his village and smashed in the roofs. Stoyan did not abandon the cannon until spring.
When Elena showed him the records, Stoyan struck the cannon with a hammer — twenty-seven times, once for every summer.

## Heroic: "Elena in the Cloud" (1914)

The first summer the cannons fell silent, the village people came out into the field and watched the sky — they were afraid without the cannons. A hailcloud
was coming down from the mountains. **Elena** strapped on her steam wings and went into the cloud — and seven more dragon-folk after her. Lightning flashed
in the cloud, and from below the people saw shadows: wings and serpent coils. An hour later the cloud broke into rain — warm, light
rain, over the fields. Elena came down into the field, her wings scorched. The people crowded around her, and the children asked to touch the mark on her shoulder.

story:pyrenean.en:
## Tragic: "The Miner's Wage" (1866–1871)

In 1866 **José** was a young miner, and the coalition engineers offered him double wages: to go down into the old caves where,
in grandmothers' tales, winged serpents sleep on treasure, and bring up the gold. José laughed at the tales. He brought up twenty-three sacks and with
the money bought a house at the bottom of the valley, for his mother. On the Night of Opening in 1871 a winged serpent flew over the valley — straight for the seal, but
in its path stood José's new house, in whose walls, as it turned out, sheets of gold had been sewn in — from his last sack.
His mother survived. The house — did not.

## Heroic: "Basajaun's Shout" (1899)

On a winter night the one-eyed giants came down into the valley where the flocks of three villages were wintering. **The Basajaun Colossus** did not yet exist. The shepherd
**Iñaki** climbed to the forest's edge and shouted — long, high, the old mountain call — just as Basajaun shouted before a storm in the tale.
Every village in the valley heard, and everyone drove their flocks up the mountain, into the caves. In the morning the giants found empty pastures. Iñaki's voice did not
come back that winter. When the Colossus was built, its voice-pipe was tuned to a recording of Iñaki's shout.

story:alps.en:
## Tragic: "The Best Hunter" (1869–1880)

**Franz** was the best hunter in the valley. In the first year of the bounty he turned in two hundred chamois skins and with the money sent his children to school in the town.
He was proud: his valley was the "cleanest". In the winter of 1880 the dragons came down into his valley for the first time, and an avalanche buried the lower
village. Franz hung up his rifle and never took it down again. **Anna** found him twenty-four years later, comparing the records, on the list — in first
place — and went to his house. Franz opened the door and said: "I know. Every winter I know."

## Heroic: "Food on the Snow" (1914)

In the first winter after the bounty was abolished, the mountain people decided to leave food for the chamois on the high pastures — as in the old days, for the ladies.
The road to the pastures ran through the dragons' territory. **Anna** took thirteen guides and hay carried on their backs, in a blizzard, at night, for three
nights. The tatzelwurms attacked three times; the ice-climbers drove them off from the rock. They left the hay on the summit. In the morning, in the snow, around the hay
were the tracks of chamois — and among them one more, small, like a human foot, but bare. No one said anything.

story:baltic.en:
## Tragic: "The Expedition's Young Artist" (1867–1914)

On the expedition of 1867 **Jaan** was a twenty-year-old artist. He drew the giant turned to stone from every side — and his hand wedged in the rock separately, on nine
sheets. When they cut the hand out, Jaan wept, because he thought he was watching the hero being freed. Forty-seven years later **Kaia**
found his drawings in the archive: nine sheets that show exactly how the hand had been placed. Old Jaan is still alive. When Kaia
showed him the drawings and explained what they needed them for, he was silent a long time. Then he said: "I was right to weep then. Only for the wrong reason."

## Heroic: "Bringing Back the Statue" (1914)

The statue of the hero turned to stone stood in the museum, in the great hall, and bringing it to the gate would take three weeks — by road, through the marshes, across enemy
territory. **Kaia** asked the townspeople for help. The next morning a thousand people stood at the museum — with ropes, carts, horses. They hauled the statue
by hand, in shifts, day and night, and the marsh beings attacked three times on the way. The statue reached the gate. Beside it now stands the Colossus —
and it is ready.

story:prussia.en:
### Tragic: "The Price of a Spoil Heap" (1866)
For twenty years **Heinrich** hauled old kobold stone from the shaft to the factory carts, and for every cart he was paid twice over — the stone was now worth
a lot. In 1866 he brought up the last heap and bought his son a house. In the spring of 1871 the brood came up through exactly that tunnel. Grete found Heinrich's
name in the factory ledger — more often than any other. Heinrich is at the front now, in a miners' detachment, hauling stone back into the shaft. For free.

### Heroic: "The Blue Charge" (1903)
The brood besieged a mining village while the shift was below. **The Blue Dragoons** rode down the valley, took the mouth of the shaft and
held it for two days until the last miner came up. To this day the village children tie blue ribbons on the horses every spring.

story:batavi.en:
### Tragic: "The Full Lake" (1852)
**Pieter** was an engineman at the great station and was proud: in three years they drained the lake, which the windmills could not have done in a century. His children
grew up on the lake bed, on a new farm. Anneke found his logbooks in the station's attic — every day, every ton of water. On the last page Pieter
had written: "Where does so much water go? The sea is not rising." No one ever answered him.

### Heroic: "Post on Skates" (1895)
In winter the fog ships cut off a frozen village from the town. Sixteen-year-old **Trijntje** skated off at night along the canals,
forty kilometres, and by morning brought back the dike-keepers. Now every winter the children race the same route — and whoever arrives first carries the post.

story:lechia.en:
### Tragic: "Skuba's Sheep" (1870)
**Wojciech** was a chemist and made the sulphur bombs. He was proud: he had turned an old tale into science. Zosia found his factory ledger —
how many bombs, in which month — and beside it the count of brood, in the same months. Wojciech studied the two columns for a long time. The next day he closed the factory
and went to the salt mine, as an ordinary miner.

### Heroic: "Wings in the Fog" (1899)
The utopiecs attacked a riverside village under cover of fog, and in the fog the village could see nothing. **The Winged Hussars** charged into the fog — the sound of the wings
carried from afar, and the villagers knew where not to fire. In the village they still say: "If you hear wings, don't be afraid."

story:byzantium.en:
### Tragic: "The Chain-Smith" (1865)
**Andronikos** forged the links of the chain and was proud: the old harbour chain, made again, of steel. His son was a sailor. In the storm of
1878 his son's ship sank in the harbour, inside the chain — it could not get out to sea. Marina found Andronikos's mark on every link of the chain.
Andronikos is with the League's smiths now: he is trying to work out how his chain can be cut.

### Heroic: "Sea Fire" (1901)
Focalor's ships were nearing the shore at night. **The Siphoneers** poured sea fire onto the water from the wall, and the fire burned on the waves
until the ships turned back. That night the people of both shores stood on the wall — all together — watching the water glitter.

story:ottoman.en:
### Tragic: "The Almanac Printer" (1868)
**Mehmed** printed the almanac's sheets at the press and was proud: the calendar printed by his hand hung in every house. Elif found his name
in the press's ledgers — the first printing, 1868. Mehmed too lost his daughter in the last thirteen nights of the zemheri. Now he writes out the old calendar
by hand, from house to house, and at every door says the same thing: "Add thirteen nights."

### Heroic: "The Karagöz Night" (1897)
On a zemheri night children were locked in a school, and voices were calling them from the street. **A Karagöz shadow-player** lit a lantern and played on the wall all night
— the quarrel of Karagöz and his friend, so funny that the children could no longer hear the voices in the street. At dawn every child
was in the school. In the city they still say: "Whoever laughs does not answer the voice."
